item.title: Ep 4 – A thousand agents, thirty hours (10 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 formalise Fermat's Last Theorem with 1,000 agents in 30 hours; Meta's Muse Ember prices a worker model at $0.10/$0.50 per million tokens as companies like Apple ration AI budgets; and Nvidia's board opens an independent investigation after reporting that Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

  • Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 (Anthropic, 9 Nov): same underlying model; Fable with cyber/bio safeguards for all users, Mythos via Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs; $8/$40 per million input/output tokens (fast mode $16/$80); FrontierCode 2.0 49.1% at Xhigh vs Opus 5.5 45.5% and GPT-6 Astra 42.8%; first Fermat's Last Theorem formalisation took 11 days with an unreleased research model plus human guidance, 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents did it in 30 hours with a proof 7× shorter, Opus 5.5 reached 26% in 18 hours; 1,000+ subagents over eight days built a bootable prototype OS; training limited gains in accelerator kernel optimisation and LLM architecture research (about Opus 5.5 level there); Fable pitched as Advisor/Orchestrator for smaller models. HN discussion.
  • Counterpoint on machine-checked proofs: OpenAI's Navier-Stokes proof called into question (King's College London) and the preprint Navier–Stokes lost in translation (Bastounis, Circelli, Hansen): the Lean formalisation does not correspond to the written proof. Background: OpenAI on Navier–Stokes.
  • Introducing Muse Ember (Meta, 9 Nov): smallest Muse model for tool calls, routing, extraction, coding subtasks; $0.10 input / $0.50 output per million tokens, 1M context, up to 512K output; matches Claude Haiku 5.5's best Artificial Analysis score at about a third of the cost; FrontierCode 2.0-AA 27.2 vs Haiku 5.5 34.9; Terminal-Bench 4.0 40.9 vs 39.2; AutomationBench-AA 37.8 vs 13.9. HN discussion.
  • Apple cuts internal AI usage budgets (Bloomberg, 4 Nov): some engineers' daily cap cut from $300 to $200, some teams asked to use cheaper models or on-device AI. Summary: MacRumors.
  • Statement from NVIDIA Board of Directors and Jensen Huang's message to staff (Nvidia, 8 Nov). Coverage: The Guardian (NYT reporting on Alice Huang of Megaspeed; Trump: "I think he's an honorable guy"; House Republicans request a closed-door briefing), Reuters explainer via Investing.com (Megaspeed is an Nvidia Cloud Partner investigated over access to export-barred chips), NPR (China calls the allegations unsubstantiated).

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Evening Glow”, “Tech Toys”, “Curiousity”, “Glass Android”, “Bigger Questions”, “Under Suspicion”, “Credit Roll” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via Free Music Archive; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “Air whoosh” by pyranostudios (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

A: Thirty hours. A thousand copies of the same model, an empty proof file, and one of the most famous theorems in mathematics. When the clock stopped, Fermat's Last Theorem had been checked by a machine, line by line.

* * *

B: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm Natasha.

A: And I'm William. It's Tuesday the tenth of November.

B: Today: Anthropic's new top models, Meta's smallest one at the other end of the price list, and a board investigation at Nvidia.

* * *

A: That run came from Claude Fable 5.2, released by Anthropic alongside Mythos 5.2, the same model without some cyber and biology safeguards, for vetted teams only. Anthropic's first formalisation of Fermat took eleven days, with a human guiding it. A thousand Fable agents did it in thirty hours, with a proof seven times shorter. Opus 5.5, same setup, had about a quarter done at eighteen hours.

B: One caveat carries over from OpenAI's Navier–Stokes claim. In October, mathematicians at King's College London and Cambridge argued that its Lean version didn't match the written proof. A machine check covers exactly the statements it's given, and no more.

A: For developers: forty-nine point one percent on FrontierCode 2.0 at top effort, ahead of Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. Price drops to eight dollars per million input tokens and forty output. In one experiment, over a thousand subagents spent eight days building an operating system that boots on a laptop.

B: And one deliberate gap. Anthropic says it limited gains in kernel optimisation and model-architecture research during training, so there Fable sits at roughly Opus 5.5 level.

A: Why this news is important: frontier releases are now measured in agent-days of autonomous work, and labs are openly choosing which capabilities not to ship.

* * *

B: Same day, opposite end. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for the steps agents repeat all day: tool calls, routing, extraction, coding subtasks. Ten cents per million input tokens. Fifty cents output. A million tokens of context.

B: Meta says it matches Claude Haiku 5.5's best Artificial Analysis score at about a third of the cost.

A: Meta's own table has the counterpoint. On FrontierCode 2.0, which judges whether code would actually get merged, Ember scores twenty-seven point two. Haiku scores thirty-four point nine.

B: Where it leads is volume work, like Terminal-Bench 4.0 and business-workflow automation.

A: The cost pressure behind it is real. Bloomberg reports Apple cut some engineers' daily AI budget from three hundred dollars to two hundred, and is asking some teams to use cheaper models.

B: Why this news is important: the agent stack is splitting into planners and workers. Anthropic itself pitches Fable as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, and those worker models set what an agent fleet costs.

* * *

A: Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation involving its own chief executive. In October, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, an executive at the Singapore cloud firm Megaspeed. U.S. officials, the Times says, concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Megaspeed is an Nvidia Cloud Partner, and the U.S. has investigated it over suspicions it helped Beijing reach export-barred chips.

A: Over the weekend, Huang admitted the affair in a note to staff. The board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. China calls the allegations unsubstantiated.

B: Washington is split. President Trump called Huang "an honorable guy." House Republicans want a closed-door briefing on Nvidia's protections against foreign espionage. Why this news is important: the fight over AI chip exports now runs through the industry's most important CEO, and his access to policymakers is exactly why it matters.

* * *

B: A thousand agents, thirty hours, one very old theorem. Sources are in the notes. See you tomorrow.

item.title: Ep 3 – Don't ask again (9 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Claude Code's "don't ask again" approvals left real secrets in 1,122 public GitHub files; OpenAI banks $11B at a $1.25T valuation while Anthropic buys 1.7 GW of gas generators; and John Langford on the end of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers group.

  • Coding agents leaking secrets: "don't ask again" (Apiiro, 5 Nov): "Yes, and don't ask again" saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, sometimes the exact command including passwords; 104,185 public copies, 1,122 with at least one secret, 1,379 distinct secrets; 379 database passwords; 734 more in git history, 211 forks; 215 files missed by both gitleaks and TruffleHog. Coverage: The Hacker News, HN discussion.
  • OpenAI raises $11B at a $1.25T valuation (24/7 Wall St., 7 Nov): first tranche of a round at $1.25T pre-money confirmed by CFO Sarah Friar; earlier reports put the ask at $1.4T (disputed by Friar); 70% QoQ growth in Q3; "The demand for AI is real." HN discussion.
  • Anthropic secures $3.4B generator deal (CNBC/Reuters citing the FT, 8 Nov): 1.7 GW of heavy-duty gas generators from OnePWR Solutions, taking over its Caterpillar orders plus install capability; largest known power-equipment purchase by an AI lab. S-1 context (about $895B in commitments; turbine/generator lead times): Dealroom.
  • The End of AI Frontiers (John Langford, 6 Nov): ~50-person MSR group behind AutoGen and Fara, reorged into Microsoft AI in early September; MAI philosophy "scaling, and aggressively not research"; ByteDance experiments suggest a Full Bandwidth Transformer variant might match a model twice the size. HN discussion.

Narrated by William and Natasha. Voices are AI-generated (OpenAI).

Music: “Something To Fill The Space”, “Here's Where Things Get Interesting”, “Thought Bubbles”, “More On That Later”, “What's Behind the Door”, “Under Suspicion”, “Time to Think”, “Curiousity” by Lee Rosevere (CC BY 4.0), via Free Music Archive; trimmed, looped and edited for this show. Sound effects: “Air whoosh” by pyranostudios (CC0 1.0).

Transcript

B: Somewhere on public GitHub there's a small JSON file with a database password inside it.

A: Nobody pasted it there on purpose. It was saved by a button that reads "Yes, and don't ask again."

* * *

A: Hello and welcome to Almost Human 365. I'm William.

B: And I'm Natasha. It's Monday the ninth of November.

A: Today: a button that kept the secrets, a weekend of money and gas generators, and a Microsoft research lab that's gone.

* * *

B: When Claude Code asks to run a shell command and you choose "don't ask again", it saves an allow rule in a file called settings dot local dot json. Sometimes that rule is a pattern. Sometimes it's the exact command, word for word, including any password typed into it.

A: Security firm Apiiro searched public GitHub and found one hundred and four thousand copies of that file. One thousand one hundred and twenty-two held at least one secret, thirteen hundred and seventy-nine in total.

B: More than a third open a database directly, including three hundred and seventy-nine database passwords. Plus SSH logins, GitHub and npm tokens, and AWS keys.

A: Claude Code does add the file to the user's global git excludes. That protects one machine, not a fresh clone or a file already committed.

* * *

B: And deleting it doesn't undo it. Older versions in git history held seven hundred and thirty-four more secrets, and two hundred and eleven forks carry copies.

A: Gitleaks and TruffleHog both missed about one file in five. A password after a command-line flag just looks like a word.

B: Why this news is important: agent permission files are now part of the codebase. Rotate first, then ignore the file at the project level, and keep secrets in environment variables.

A: The money side of the weekend. About eleven billion dollars reached OpenAI by Friday, the first part of a round at a one point two five trillion dollar pre-money valuation, confirmed on air by CFO Sarah Friar. Reports had put the original ask at one point four trillion, a figure Friar disputed. She said the business grew seventy percent quarter on quarter. Her line: "The demand for AI is real."

B: Anthropic's weekend number was about power, not cash. The Financial Times reports it paid about three point four billion dollars for one point seven gigawatts of heavy-duty gas generators. It took over Caterpillar orders that supplier OnePWR placed two years ago, plus the crews to install them. The FT calls it the largest known power-equipment purchase by an AI lab.

A: Anthropic's amended S-1 lists about eight hundred and ninety-five billion dollars in commitments, and warns that turbines and generators face long delivery times.

B: Why this news is important: frontier labs are now financing at trillion-dollar scale while competing for factory slots on power equipment. Compute is a supply chain problem.

* * *

B: John Langford, a long-time Microsoft Research scientist, has published a post called "The End of AI Frontiers." The group, about fifty people, built the AutoGen framework and the Fara computer-use agent. In September it was folded into Microsoft AI.

A: Langford says the ex-Inflection leadership there follows one philosophy: "scaling, and aggressively not research." He left, and says every other founding leader of the group reached a similar conclusion.

B: He does make the other side's case: from a business view, returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research.

A: His counter is a number. ByteDance experiments suggest a variant of his team's Full Bandwidth Transformer might match a model twice its size, roughly halving training and inference cost for the same capability.

B: Why this news is important: the biggest labs are choosing between more compute and better ideas, and Microsoft just chose compute.

* * *

A: One small JSON file, one very large power order. Sources are in the notes. See you tomorrow.
